1:
The reply is a retort, and two voices say so. Gill has him rise as soon as Eliphaz had finished. Henry describes the pattern both had fallen into, each undervaluing the other's sense, and warns that the longer the saw of contention is drawn the hotter it grows: the censure Eliphaz passed on Job's discourses is the one Job now passes on his, which is easy and endless and does no good, stirring the passions without convincing the judgment. Ellicott reads the speech as an abandonment of argument: finding the dispute useless, the sufferer complains of its conduct, contrasts their treatment of him with what he would have given them, enlarges on his condition, appeals to heaven, and ends by calling his case desperate. Gregory the Great reads it as a pattern of something larger. He takes it for a peculiar way with the wicked to charge their own faults on the good before anyone charges them, so that while they dread reproach they testify that the righteous who withstand them do the same; holy men bear even accusations they cannot remember deserving, and when they cannot correct such men by preaching they endure them, to win the reward of long patience where they cannot win a conversion. He finds the Church's voice in the psalm about sinners plowing upon her back, since in bearing with those she cannot correct she carries their deeds; and this sufferer, faced with a friend who turned words of comfort into bitter upbraiding, maintains by his patience a type of the Church.

On the staleness of the speech they are unanimous and various. Gill has heard such sayings from his teachers and parents many times over, so that nothing new was offered, only the same dish cooked again, which is not merely needless but nauseous. Keil and Delitzsch grant the speech was meant for comfort but call it primarily an accusation that wounds instead of soothing, and render the phrase as troublesome comforters, men who cause trouble instead of relieving it. Clarke's paraphrase turns it into an accusation of pretence: the sayings of the ancients are familiar but do not fit the case, and men who see a sufferer and do not console him should not claim to be consoling. Ellicott calls the matter trite rather than true, or at least less than the whole truth, and quotes a line about the common commonplace and vacant chaff well meant for grain. Wesley makes the same judgment and extends it, since to a soul under deep conviction of sin or the arrest of death all creatures are equally trivial. Henry separates two faults: needless repetition, provoking from an adversary but often necessary from a teacher, since precept must be upon precept; and unskilful application, where men who came to comfort mistook the case entirely, so that the patient's medicines were poisons and his physicians his worst disease.

The wish that vain words would end leads into the hardest stroke of the speech. Gill glosses them as words of wind, swelling bubbles that look big and hold nothing, and advises that men who can speak to no better purpose had better be silent. Clarke renders the phrase words of air and turns the next question on Eliphaz as ignorant of the business. Ellicott prefers an interrogative with the negative, shall not vain words have an end, and notes that the last reply only reiterated what had been said already. Henry draws out the request to change places: it is no absurd supposition, since the turns of the wheel are such that the spokes soon change places, and we ought to make our brethren's sorrows our own because we do not know how soon they may be. His closing observations are that it is easy to trample on those who are down, and that good words cost nothing and may yet make broken bones rejoice.
4:
The offer to change places is where the three commentators part company. Gill hears it as a threat not carried out: the sufferer could have spoken as big, with as high a tone and as stiff a neck, and he turns the clause into two questions, whether he ought to speak so and whether he would, answering that his conscience would not let him. Clarke prefers to render the verbs as plain futures, with Mr. Good, so that the sense is, I also will speak; and he fills in what such speaking would be, a man quoting wise sayings to prove his friends hypocrites, and where he did not care to assert outright, shaking his head to insinuate that much more lay behind. Clarke's two rhetorical questions, whether that would be fair and whether it would be right, carry his judgement, and he adds that a saying's being in the memory is no proof that it was made for this case or applies to it. Ellicott raises the real crux. He notes that the head-shaking may be read either in contrast with the next verse, as the English version takes it, or in parallel with it, so that the whole couplet is sympathy rather than mockery — making oneself a companion, condoling, shaking the head as a mark of fellow-feeling. He supports the possibility by observing that the phrase here is not quite the phrase used elsewhere, where shaking the head is plainly contempt and derision.

The promise to strengthen them is read two opposite ways as well. Gill takes it at face value and expands it devotionally: God strengthens his people by answering them with comfortable words, an angel strengthened Christ as man in his agony, and one saint may strengthen another in distress — as this sufferer had strengthened others in former times, by the admission of Eliphaz himself, and would again if his circumstances changed. Clarke reports Mr. Good's very different rendering, that with his own mouth he would overpower them until the quivering of his lips should fail, for which Mr. Good contends in his learned notes. Clarke notes that this translation is countenanced by the Septuagint, Syriac and Arabic versions, which makes the clause a threat of unanswerable speech rather than a promise of comfort.

The sixth verse states a double bind, and Henry sets it out best. He observes that the sufferer is at a stand whether to smother his complaint or give it vent, since both relieve the afflicted in their turn and neither relieved him. Speaking gave no ease, because his spirit was never the lighter for pouring out the complaint and what he said was misconstrued into an aggravation of his grief. Silence gave no ease either, because forbearing brought him no nearer anything; and Henry's summary of the trap is exact — if he complained he was censured as passionate, if he kept silence as sullen; if he maintained his integrity that was made his crime, and if he answered nothing his silence was taken for a confession of guilt. Gill reaches the same place by a different route, distinguishing speech to God in prayer, which got no abatement of his sorrows, from speech to himself in soliloquy, which did not repress them, so that a man who could comfort others could not comfort himself. Clarke puts it in a line, that reprehending his friends' conduct will not mitigate his sufferings. Ellicott puts it in half of one: he cannot but reply, though replying gives him no relief.
7:
The weariness is traced to its author with some hesitation. Gill allows that the subject may be the grief itself but prefers God, on the strength of the next clause, and describes a man made weary of the world and of life by afflictions heavier than the sand of the sea. Wesley agrees and offers two objects for the weariness, complaining or living. Ellicott notices the grammatical oscillation that runs through the passage, since the sufferer alternately speaks of God in the third person and addresses him in the second, and he reads the desolation as covering both the destruction of the children and the alienation of the friends. Clarke reports the Latin version, which makes the grief the oppressor and the joints reduced to nothing, and adds the detail that hurts most, that not a single child was left to continue the name or comfort an old age; he also records Mr. Good's rendering, that all the sufferer's witnesses have been struck apart. Keil and Delitzsch spend their note on the verb of the next verse, which occurs only once besides and whose primary sense is grasping firmly, from which both comprehending and wrinkling have branched; they take wrinkling as the sense here, since the emaciation mentioned after it, and the picture of a man sick with elephantiasis, show what the poet had in view.

The wrinkles are a witness, and the question is a witness to what. Gill refers them to affliction rather than age, which had sunk the flesh and furrowed it so that the man looked older than he was, and he adds the distinction that this is said of the body, since the soul, through grace, was without spot or wrinkle. Clarke thinks the words would apply most forcibly if the disease was the elephantiasis, where the whole skin wrinkles like an elephant's hide, which is what gave that leprosy its name. He grants the passage is obscure and variously rendered, and quotes Houbigant for a version in which the witness is a liar who rises against the sufferer and contradicts him to his face. Ellicott takes the plainer and harsher sense, that the wrinkles witnessed against him, and that in his friends' eyes they furnished unquestionable proof of his guilt.

Who it is that tears him in wrath divides the commentators four ways. Gill rejects both Jarchi's Satan and the suggestion that Eliphaz is meant, and takes it of God — guarding the reading at once, since this was a mistaken apprehension of a God who hates none of his creatures, however hateful sin is to him. Ellicott agrees and admits how far it goes, since the sufferer here calls God his adversary and so almost exceeds his own earlier language; it is hardly possible to understand it otherwise, because God is openly named just afterwards. Clarke refuses both the usual answers and offers a third: that God permitted Satan to show himself, and that the horrible form which he and his demons assumed increased the misery. On that principle Clarke reads the whole passage consistently, the gnashing teeth and sharpened eyes belonging to the tempter, the gaping mouths to his demons, and the delivering up to the ungodly meaning a man abandoned to be tortured by them. His argument is that referring these expressions to three human friends strains the figures to an insufferable height. Keil and Delitzsch divide the passage instead, taking the mockers not for the friends but for the neighbours who had envied his prosperity and now rejoice at his fall, men to whom his uprightness had been a burden and who count themselves rid of a censorious and over-righteous lord. They add that the perfects are not present but describe the change his suffering has wrought. Wesley's note is smallest and most vivid: a fierce and sparkling eye such as enraged men turn on their enemies.
10:
The gaping mouths are referred to the friends, and both voices who treat the verse take it typologically. Gill identifies them as the instruments God allowed to use him ill, men who came at him open-mouthed with calumnies and charges he was not conscious of, and whose gesture was itself a form of contempt. He then carries the whole verse over to Christ, on whom the reproach of those that reproached God fell, who was laughed to scorn with the lip shot out and the head shaken, and against whom mouths were opened like a ravening and roaring lion when the cry went up to crucify him. Wesley makes the same identification in two words, my friends, and the same application at more length, citing the psalm where they gape with their mouths and the prophecy about smiting the judge of Israel on the cheek.

Being handed over to the ungodly raises the question who they were. Gill lays out four candidates for a word that stands in the singular: Satan, into whose hands the man's person had been given with only his life reserved — against which Gill objects that the sufferer did not yet know it; Eliphaz; the friends collectively, if the singular stands for a plural; or the raiders who had carried off his substance. He then applies the clause to Christ delivered to the Gentiles by the determinate counsel of God, and notes that the verb may also mean shut up or delivered bound, which was literally true in that case. Wesley makes the same application in one line. Ellicott keeps to the speaker's own situation and hears a retort: ungodly and wicked are the words thrown back at the friends, and he thinks they had earned them.

The contrast of former ease with present breaking is drawn out by all four. Gill describes the two kinds of ease that were lost, affluent circumstances in which a man lay quietly in his nest expecting to die there, and peace of conscience in which he trusted his living Redeemer and enjoyed the light of God's countenance; against which he sets four breakings, of substance, of family, of body by boils and ruptures, and of spirit under a sense of divine displeasure. He also records Mr. Broughton's blunter rendering, that a wealthy man has been undone. Keil and Delitzsch work the two intensive verbs, one meaning to break up entirely and crumble in pieces, the other to beat or dash in pieces, and read the sequence as a man seized by the neck, lifted up, and dashed down. Wesley supplies the human comparison for the shaking, a strong man wrestling with a stripling, and reads the setting up as a mark as being made a target for every arrow. Ellicott calls the passage highly poetical and gives it the one image a reader remembers, the sufferer become a St. Sebastian for the arrows of God, with no more vivid picture conceivable of a man under the persecuting hand of the Almighty.
13:
The archers are identified several ways, and the word itself is disputed. Gill offers four: Satan and his powers with their fiery darts, the friends shooting bitter words, the diseases of the body so many arrows lodged in every part of him, and behind all of these the arrows of the Almighty felt as wrath. He carries the figure to Christ through the blessing on Joseph, where the archers sorely grieved him, and reports Gussetius for a rendering that makes them his great ones, which fits friends who were men of substance. Clarke gives the same alternative sense and then the versions, the Latin and Greek making them spears, the Syriac, Arabic and Chaldee arrows. His most useful note is Mr. Heath's, that the whole passage is a hunting metaphor taken in order: the beast is first surrounded, then shot dead, then opened and emptied, then broken up limb by limb. Wesley's note is a rule rather than a gloss, that whoever our enemies are we must see them as God's archers and God as directing the arrow. Gill reads the breach upon breach of the next verse as the blows on substance, family and health that came thick and fast, one messenger of ill news on the back of another.

The sackcloth sewn to the skin is taken by three of them as a medical detail. Keil and Delitzsch point out that he does not say he put the coarse cloth on or wrapped himself in it but that he sewed it upon his naked body, which they attribute to the distortion caused by elephantiasis, that will not admit ordinary clothes; and the word used is not the common one for skin but one meaning the scurfy, scaly surface. Ellicott takes it the other way and makes the skin itself the comparison, hardened and rugged as sackcloth, on the ground that the second half of the verse must be figurative and there is no reason to read the first half differently. Gill keeps it literal and voluntary, put on when the mantle was rent, like the king of Nineveh's sackcloth, and rejects the suggestion that the man had no other clothes left; he also notes the Jewish opinion that the word means the delicate skin drawn over a healing wound, which would make such rough stuff very hard to bear. Wesley reads the whole act as self-abasement, the answer to a charge of stretching out the hand against God, and sees in the sewing a resolve to keep the humiliation up as long as the affliction lasted.

The horn defiled in the dust is where Clarke's note runs longest. He takes the horn for an emblem of power borrowed from the beasts whose strength lies there, notes that horns were worn on crowns and helmets as ancient coins show, and says the ornament is still part of the diadem of the kings and chiefs of Abyssinia. For that he quotes Mr. Bruce's travels, which describe a broad fillet bound round a governor's forehead with a gilt silver cone some four inches long set in the middle, called by a word answering to horn and worn only at parades after a victory. Clarke keeps Bruce's shrewdest observation, that a man wearing it holds his neck crookedly for fear the thing should tip forward, which explains the psalm's rebuke about speaking with a stiff neck while the horn is held on high. Rolling that ornament in the dust therefore signifies the disgrace and destruction of power and eminence. Clarke rejects Mr. Good's rendering, which makes it a turban rolled in the dust, since the Hebrew word is the same as the Ethiopic one naming exactly what Bruce saw. Wesley says in a sentence what the note establishes, that the man had willingly parted with wealth, power and glory, and was content to lie in the dust.
16:
The foulness of the face is a question of colour. Gill lists what the weeping was for — the loss of substance and especially of children, the unkindness of friends, the man's own corruptions, and the hiding of God's face — and then notes that the word carries the sense of redness in Arabic, used of red wine and, as Schultens adds, of its fermenting, which fits a face swollen and red with excessive tears. Ellicott says the same in six words, that red, as with wine, is probably better than foul. Keil and Delitzsch reject the rendering that makes the eyes kindled, which the Greek and Latin took from a root meaning to ferment, and prefer the root that names the Alhambra for its redness: the eyes are reddened all over with weeping, and so weakened that the shadow of death seems to rest on the eyelids. Clarke reads that shadow as a prognosis, death now fast approaching and his shadow already thrown over the man. Keil and Delitzsch add the observation that gives the verse its edge, that all this misery belongs to someone who is no disguised hypocrite with penance to do in sackcloth and ashes and no solace in his tears; and they reject an attempt to make the next clause a prepositional phrase about the absence of evil in his hands, since the clauses there are substantival.

The denial that follows is carefully bounded. Gill marks what is not being claimed: not that there was no sin in his heart or life, which he had acknowledged already, but that nothing in his hands had been got unjustly — no man's property taken, no private injury done, and no justice perverted as a magistrate by taking bribes or favouring persons, a charge he could challenge anyone to prove as Samuel once did. Clarke makes it a dying assertion, that the friends' charges are groundless and that a man afflicted to death is not afflicted for his iniquities. Wesley adds the positive half, that the sufferer has not cast off the fear and service of God but prays and worships still, and with a sincere heart. Ellicott takes the clause literally as for no injustice, and compares a verse in Isaiah where the English because he had done no violence should rather be not because he had done any violence.

Henry treats the verse as the one support the sufferer had left, and divides the conscience two ways. Towards men, the claim is that no wealth was unjustly got or kept, which answers Eliphaz's picture of a tyrant and an oppressor: the man had never wronged anybody and had always despised the gain of oppression. Towards God, the claim is that the prayer is pure — and Henry makes the two halves depend on each other, since prayer cannot be pure while there is injustice in the hands. He observes that Eliphaz's charge had been hypocrisy in religion and that the answer names prayer, the great act of religion, professing purity in it not from all infirmity but from reigning and allowed guile, unlike the prayers of men who look no further than being seen. Henry's balance is the fairest thing in his comment: nobody was ever readier to own sins of infirmity, and yet on search the man could charge himself with no enormous crime that would account for his being made more miserable than other men. The comfort Henry draws from it is that the testimony of conscience is a real support, though he will add at once that a witness in our own bosom stands us in little stead without a witness in heaven, since God is greater than our hearts and we are not to be our own judges.
18:
The appeal to the earth is read in two incompatible ways, and Clarke sets them out before choosing. On the first the words call for vengeance against the sufferer's destroyers: his blood is his life, taken from him by violence, and he asks that it cry against them as Abel's cried against Cain, the ground not being suffered to hide a murder. On the second, which Clarke takes from Mr. Scott's verse rendering and from Mr. Good, the man supposes himself accused of murder and, conscious of being guiltless, prays that no drop shed by him may lie concealed. Clarke prefers the first, with deference to both scholars, on the ground that the Hebrew will not support the second and that no ancient version read it so; and he thinks the first quite in character for a man in impassioned querulousness. Gill and Wesley take the second line. Gill makes the whole a curse on himself: if he were guilty of a capital crime, let his own gore find no burial but be licked up, and let whatever sins deserve that name — the shedding of life, which he doubts the friends even suspected, or the grinding of the poor — stand published rather than hidden. Wesley puts it in one clause: if I am guilty of destroying any man, let the earth bring it to light.

The clause about the cry is construed in opposite directions. Ellicott takes it as a prayer for the widest hearing: no corner of the world the outcry fails to reach, and no resting-place where it might settle and be forgotten. Wesley takes it as the other half of the curse: if the charge were true, let his complaints to men and his petitions to God alike find no room in any ear or heart.

The witness in heaven is where the chapter turns. Gill identifies him as the God whose throne is above, who observes every deed of the sons of men, and notes that the appeal cuts both ways by design: let him testify against the man if guilty, and for him if not, which is what he expects. Clarke reduces it to a sentence, an appeal to God for his innocence, while Wesley sets conscience beside it, so that the man holds two attestations, his own and God's. Ellicott makes the most of it. He treats such passages as the preparation for the famous confession later in the book, and asks what more a believer in the full light of the Gospel could say, knowing of One in heaven who ever makes intercession — and yet this faith had already risen to that height and grasped that hope. His verdict is that no other book of the Bible shows faith clinging to the all-just God for justification as this one does. Keil and Delitzsch give the verses without comment at this point, letting the rendering stand.
20:
What the friends scorned is worth distinguishing, and Gill distinguishes it. They did not, he says, mock the man's diseases and calamities, which would have been brutish and inhuman, but his words — the arguments and reasons he had used in his own defence. Clarke keeps the two halves of the verse together, derision on their side and a steady look toward God on his, from whom he expects his cause to be vindicated. Ellicott proposes reading the clause as an apostrophe, so that the sufferer turns and addresses them: you who scorn me and yet profess, and ought, to be my friends. On that construction the tears poured out to God have a purpose attached, that he would maintain the right of a man against God and of a son of man against his neighbour; and Ellicott notes that this is the longing already expressed earlier in the book.

The plea itself asks for something the speaker knows is not ordinarily granted. Gill offers three forms of it: that someone might be appointed and allowed to plead with God on his behalf, or that he might be admitted to plead for himself, or at least that his case might come to a hearing where God would decide the controversy between him and his friends — which he had no doubt would be decided his way. Ellicott's alternative rendering turns the same request into a comparison, that one might plead for man with God as a son of man pleads for his neighbour, which puts the wanted arbiter in human terms.

The closing verse about the numbered years is textually and critically the busiest in the chapter. Gill offers the usual senses, that a man's years are few at best and these fewer still in the sufferer's apprehension, or that they are years of number in the sense of being fixed and allotted, or simply few enough to count. Ellicott gives both constructions and compares the idiom where men of number means few men, then raises a difficulty of his own: it is strange to hear a man in this condition speak of years at all, as strange as to find one so sorely tormented sustaining so long an argument — which he suggests may show that the narrative is meant as an ideal rather than a record. Clarke takes the harder line on the text, preferring Mr. Good's rendering that the years numbered to him have come and he must go the way of no return, since a man expecting death hourly could not look for a few more years of life. He argues from this that the first verse of the next chapter belongs here, and that the received translation of this one is therefore improper. Clarke also returns to his earlier claim, that part of these sufferings arose from appalling representations made to the eye or the imagination by Satan and his agents, which he maintains is neither irrational nor improbable, such power having been credited in every age. Wesley reads the journey plainly as the going to the place of the dead from which no one returns, and draws the practical conclusion the speech has been working toward: death hastens, and therefore the case between him and his friends should be determined now — so that if he is guilty he may bear the shame before all men, and if innocent he may see both his own integrity and the credit of religion cleared.
